assumptions: The candidate initially targets importers above the applicable threshold whose supplier complexity and expected value from actual emissions data are sufficient to justify managed-service spend.
The founder remains employed and can commit no more than five hours per day until objective traction, positive contribution economics, repeatable demand, and adequate runway are established.
The cited competitor pricing represents software rather than an equivalent fully managed service, so it is treated as price pressure rather than a complete price ceiling.
Importer mandates, supplier permissions, specialist support, and accredited verification are potentially obtainable but are not assumed signed, exclusive, or durable.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: The highest-value evidence would be several paid importer audits followed by at least one managed-service conversion, with documented buyer and budget owner, contract price, sales cycle, CAC, supplier response and defect rates, hours per supplier, specialist and verifier costs, insurance cost, contribution margin, cash collection, and renewal intent. Signed importer data and outreach rights plus a broker referral agreement, and measured certificate savings or workload reduction versus default values and low-priced software, would materially improve the assessment.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: The shift from transitional reporting to certificate-bearing CBAM operation creates a real link between poor emissions data, compliance work, and importer cash exposure. The insight is strong, though default emissions values mean supplier-level actual-data collection is not universally necessary.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Regulatory deadlines, certificate costs, and a named importer using an external CBAM solution support genuine pain and an external-buying event. However, there is no candidate-specific paid validation, disclosed contract value, or proof that mid-market importers will pay the proposed managed-service price rather than use defaults, brokers, or inexpensive software.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Upfront onboarding plus annual recurring fees could provide favorable cash conversion and repeat work, but every decisive economic input remains assumed: price, CAC, onboarding effort, supplier-response workload, specialist and verifier costs, insurance, margin, retention, and payback. The public £199-£699 monthly software substitute also pressures the proposed 15,000-80,000 PLN annual range unless human service delivers clearly greater value.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Mid-market EU importers in covered sectors form an identifiable regulatory segment, but the beachhead is not yet narrowed by geography, commodity, supplier complexity, certificate exposure, or ERP maturity. The 50-tonne exemption removes the vast majority of importers and shifts the opportunity toward fewer, larger accounts likely to attract established vendors.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: A focused multilingual supplier-operations service could serve accounts poorly handled by enterprise systems, but the candidate owns neither the buyer relationship nor an essential workflow. Brokers can white-label existing tools, CBAMable offers a direct substitute, and SAP can bundle CBAM into systems already holding trade, supplier, and accounting data.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: Successful supplier-data operations could extend across additional CBAM sectors and EU geographies and into adjacent emissions, trade-compliance, document-validation, and certificate-forecasting workflows. Expansion is plausible but depends on earning reusable rights, expertise, and channel access that are not presently secured.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Response benchmarks, document mappings, and multilingual playbooks could improve operations over time, but no reusable permissioned dataset, exclusive agreement, durable retention right, switching cost, or learning-rate advantage is evidenced. Source data, accredited verification, the official registry, and customer access remain externally controlled.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: Done-for-you supplier chasing and provenance management may be more convenient than self-service software and more accessible than enterprise suites. Yet there is no measured superiority in certificate savings, response rate, accuracy, implementation time, or total cost, so the advantage is presently a credible service proposition rather than a demonstrated behavior-changing offer.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: Timing is favorable because the definitive regime began in 2026, certificate prices create visible financial exposure, and importers now face implementation work and future declarations. The same regulatory activation also accelerates entry by brokers, specialist software vendors, and enterprise incumbents.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: Customs brokers, freight forwarders, associations, and targeted importer lists are plausible routes, but there is no pipeline, referral agreement, conversion evidence, or repeatable acquisition result. Brokers may prefer to own and white-label the workflow themselves, creating both channel conflict and dependence for a founder who is less suited to sustained relationship-heavy selling.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: A fixed-fee audit can be launched within the founder's capital and analytical capabilities, with AI supporting data and workflow automation. Delivery nevertheless requires carbon-methodology expertise, accredited verifier coordination, multilingual supplier operations, security, liability management, and dependable supplier cooperation; 20-25 weekly hours also reaches the founder's stated part-time limit before early hiring.

highest_value_structural_change: Concentrate on one commodity-and-geography segment where actual verified emissions predictably save customers substantially more than the service costs, then secure a broker distribution partnership and standardized multi-year importer mandate that grants durable permission to retain and reuse anonymized workflow benchmarks. This would align value, acquisition, and compounding data advantage instead of relying on a generic supplier desk.
main_structural_strength: A mandatory, recurring regulatory workflow is now tied to measurable certificate expenditure, allowing a low-capital managed-service wedge to solve a concrete importer problem before substantial software investment.
primary_score_limiter: The candidate lacks control of customer access, source data, verification, or a defensible workflow while fully loaded unit economics and willingness to pay remain unvalidated against inexpensive specialist software, broker bundling, SAP, and the option to use default values.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: The combined adverse evidence is that the 50-tonne exemption removes the vast majority of importers, CBAMable already offers supplier-evidence and broker-white-label workflows for £199-£699 per month, and SAP bundles the process end to end; meanwhile importers can use default values and actual emissions require independent accredited verification. This materially weakens the assumed broad market, pricing power, channel ownership, indispensability, and defensibility.
